To work on difficulties or cultivate positive qualities (love, curiosity, play, confidence, etc.), simply do these steps, in order: 1) Attention; 2) Notice; 3) Offer one fitting response; 4) Wait; 5) Come all the way back. Not much needs to happen in each session!

This is a borrowed figure, so you’re still making the choice. The longer version of this exercise can be found in my Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide.

Deciding to do it. How will you coax yourself to do this? Make it spacious? Make it warm and held? Something else? Preview what you are going to do: will you close your eyes? Will you come out and go back in again? What will you do at the end? If you are going to use a recording, read the script if you can. Know that you can say stop at any time and the induction will end. If you want to change something, say less if you want it to be asking for less from you, or quiet and the talking will stop. You can also just open your eyes and stop, and then come all the way back anyway. You don't need to ask any parts for permission to stop, even if a part tells you that you do.

Let your response guide you as to what to do next regardless of what the script is expecting. Utilize. Use what you have to go to the next place, whatever it is. Learn how to notice what is there. Learn how to notice if there is no change, and that that is not a positive change. For more on language you can use, see Appendix B, or keep reading below for information on using the tools after induction in Let the next response guide you. Either way, keep the instructions about how to stay safe and how to get out plain.

Ending the session. Don’t feel that you have to end the session with a ‘great revelation’! When you have done as much as you want to do, it is a good idea to find out if there is anything that you need to do to make sure that you can leave things where they are for the time being. This might include thanking parts for their help, or making sure that you do something ‘in real life’ (eat a good meal, put a boundary in place, get some rest, repair a relationship, keep a promise etc) or it may be that there is nothing to do!

This is very similar to implementation intention. I'm not aware of research into implementation intention for this specific thing, but the general mechanisms appear to work; Gollwitzer’s paper explains how and why they work.

Somatic experiencing: If you would like more information about somatic experiencing, or even a free intro session, please see my somatic guide. In somatic experiencing (SE), you are not thrusting into the trauma. You learn to track. So you might start by tracking, by discovering where the activation is, where a neutral place is, and then whether you can move your attention from one to the other, very slowly, like a snail.

Healing the Divided Self, Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick, (1995) pp 24-27, 45-50, 83-90, covers a lot of aspects of this post, such as interactive hypnosis, helping the subject learn how to learn by using other senses, learning self hypnosis, making sure the subject comes back at the end, etc. However, this is a professional clinical book, not a self help book, so be careful about trying to use the procedures used with the cases, etc in this book for solo work (the same applies to historical information it contains). Also, Adam Eason's work with Benjamin Parris in the International Society of Hypnosis, specifically his article about self hypnosis, should be a useful thing to read (especially the parts that talk about how to learn to learn when you're directing it yourself, and about whether you need another person to help you, and using recordings to help you, etc.)

For information about using indirect hypnotic language patterns, such as pacing, utilizing, metaphor, and associational cues, etc, see Healing the Divided Self, Phillips and Frederick, 1995, pp 53 - 57, 96 - 100, as well as nimja's tutorial on hypnotic language patterns, and his tutorial on triggers. The information on these techniques comes from these sources, not because they are necessarily validating the validity of some aspects of NLP, or because every example suits trauma work (nimja did not write or endorse this guide), but because I was adapting the language used for my own purposes, and I deliberately used a sequence that would be easy to use for re-entry.

NOTE: Some of the information in this post comes from In an Unspoken Voice, Peter Levine, 2010, especially ch 5 and 7, as well as ch 3 and 4 of Freedom from Pain, Levine and Maggie Phillips 2012, and ch 4 of Healing Trauma, by Levine. These sources talk about the key concepts of tracking what is happening in the body, resources, titration, pendulation, and the range of foci available when working, from sensation and imagery to behavior, emotions, and meaning, etc. This is not done from a position of "here is what you need to do to physiologically fix it", but here are some things you can try, etc.

For information about all of these things, see Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide. The practices in this post are designed to match with those in the guide, but include some elements of learning to get into self hypnosis, as well as other helpful language, and making sure you come back at the end, etc.

Some of the information in this post is taken from Healing the Divided Self, Phillips and Frederick, 1995, pp 148-153, 171-174, about renurturing work, and how it can be combined with somatic work, and how to develop capacities for nurturing, etc. For information about attunement, and how every child is different and needs to be responded to differently, see Trauma Through a Child's Eyes, Levine and Maggie Kline, especially ch 4, 5, 10, etc, as it talks about actual kids (and this guide is applying this to how to respond to younger feeling states within an adult). The sequence for doing this with borrowed adulthood and the arrangement of 3 functions of adulthood, etc, is not from these authors, however.

Not everybody has an inner voice, Nedergaard and Lupyan 2024, is not about self hypnosis adaptations, but about people with different amounts of inner speech. The questions in the quick start are not a validated way of seeing if you can do self hypnosis, but are simply there as a practical way of seeing for yourself how you are.

Chapter 7 of Trauma and Memory, by Peter Levine, 2015, contains useful information on this. This US Veterans Administration website, contains useful general information about hypnosis, such as the fact that it can be very strong and should be carefully used, and that it may result in false memories. This ASCH website, contains information about the usefulness of getting certified in hypnosis, and why it doesn't guarantee competence. Links are available for these and other useful groups in the evidence and specialist sections, but they point to their particular claims, not every use of hypnosis.

items.title: Your little one, and they/them
items.where: Love doesn’t have to wait for trust, P1
items.my_version:
What if your little one doesn't believe you love them? It is possible to love them even if they don't believe you love them. It is possible for trust to question your promises, remember when you failed to protect them, and take it's time.

Then respond to the complaints that are sure to come. Because even if they are coming from a place that is not completely "right," there will likely be something true in what they are saying. Do what you can to show your love for them. This might include some or all of the following: Learning to listen to them when they are angry without hitting back. Owning what was not okay. Working on changing yourself so that you are less likely to turn on them. Finding other ways to make up to them for what you did. Finding other ways to show your love for them (this might include taking care of them, such as by buying and cooking food for them, setting limits for them, taking them to the doctor when they need it, and doing what you said you would do). Just not hitting back is not enough. You need to love your little one.

Be aware of what you are teaching your other positions. For example, are you teaching your little one that you are going to love them no matter what? Or are you teaching them that it is their responsibility to believe your love for them, and that if they don't, it is their fault? Is it two separate positions, one making the vow to love your little one no matter what, and the other blaming your little one for not taking in your love? Or is it one position doing both of these things? Or are you blending them? It might not be chronological age.

items.my_version: Is this a notice or meaning? "My stomach went tight" is a notice, "He's a complete bastard" is a meaning, even if you didn't think it in words. You can then go on to find out what he did, notice what it was that gave you the idea, and consider if there might be other explanations. It's also ok to put words to something you didn't think in words - if something comes up that you're analyzing, it's still good to analyze it, even if it hasn't turned into words in your head. Nonverbal thoughts and early thoughts aren't necessarily any better or worse than other thoughts. Feelings are good to pay attention to, but it's still good to consider what they mean.

items.title: "We do this on purpose"
items.where: Installing the synchronicity cue, P11
items.my_version: A downside of synchronicity cues is that they can lead to false positives. We create an association in our head on purpose when we rehearse what to do when we notice a synchronicity; however, when you are absorbed in something and/or when you are destabilized, you might think that you saw a synchronicity when in fact there wasn't any. items.my_version: Gendlin Focusing: Focusing is another approach where you work with your body. You might say to yourself, “What is the felt sense of this whole anxiety?” Don’t answer with your head; let your body come up with a vague sense of the whole anxiety. Then ask, “What would this felt sense want me to know?” Try a word or a phrase and see how well it fits the felt sense. But also see if what the word or phrase says is true of the situation. The word may feel ok, but say something that doesn’t fit the situation, or vice versa. Use the words and the body to mutually correct one another.

items.my_version: We can not ‘force’ forgiveness on ourselves, it has to come from a place of understanding otherwise it can be bypassing. However, if we remain in the anger forever, we are allowing the injury to dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it, and our boundary with them still matters, but one day we may find that we have forgiven them, or at least that we’re not being run by the resentment anymore. And we don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better.

items.title: The second half of the floating sentence
items.where: 2. Supported floating, P1
items.my_version: Supported Floating: Work out what is supporting you and where your weight is, imagine that the support is holding a tiny bit (1%) more of your effort. It’s like floating but you don’t have to lose contact, or you can just keep it at the same level, with just enough weight/pressure. See what happens, you can fractionate this if you want, perhaps noticing your normal awareness when you breathe in and the support when you breathe out. Tell yourself you are going to do this before you do it. What can you hear more easily now? Bring yourself back to normal feeling of support and return.

items.where: 3. Rhythmic breath or pulse, P1
items.my_version: Rhythmic: Use your breathing or slightly hum in your throat to make a natural rhythm, or tap your finger or listen to sounds outside to make an artificial one. You can even do it by counting to yourself (silently) or with no rhythm at all. Tell yourself you are going to say “here, and here again” over and over, and notice what you pay attention to in between the phrases, then stop saying it. Notice what you become aware of in the first beat after you stop saying it – you don’t need to make your mind blank, just notice what comes up. Does it make any words, feelings, needs or actions more clear? Bring back your normal rhythm and return.

items.my_version: Unwinding Object: Good for when you have a few different strands to one thing you want to work on. Imagine an object unwinding into its separate strands – maybe some yarn, some bubbles, or some knots – and place each strand beside you. items.title: Lined up with "Close the Session and Return to Life"
items.where: 7. Care workshop, P1
items.my_version: Care workshop: prepare the workshop (time, place, tools, boundaries, etc). Invite the signal/feeling/young part to come only as close as is welcome. Try to avoid any language that makes you not one person. Care for it as best you can, by asking what it wants and giving that if you can, or sensing into it and responding, or just being with it. Take breaks, get back in contact if that's ok, take more breaks, etc. Keep bringing in adult functions (or borrow someone else's function). Have the adult part of you run the show. Goal is to make it "good as you", not to erase history. Tell your little one, "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." Close the workspace, reassure yourself that you are one whole person, that you're an adult now, and come back.
